lesson.title: Crossing Over: How Homologous Chromosomes Swap DNA
lesson.summary: Crossing over is the exchange of DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis, creating chromatids with new combinations of alleles.
lesson.body:
Once homologous chromosomes have paired up during synapsis and formed a tetrad held together by the synaptonemal complex, something remarkable happens inside that tightly bundled structure. The DNA of one chromatid can break at a matching point on a neighboring chromatid, and the two broken ends are rejoined to the wrong partner. The result is a physical exchange of chromosome segments between two of the four chromatids in the tetrad. This process is called crossing over, and it always happens between non-sister chromatids, meaning one chromatid from the maternal homolog and one from the paternal homolog, never between the two identical sister chromatids of the same chromosome, since swapping identical DNA would change nothing.

It helps to ask why a cell would do this at all. During meiosis, whole chromosomes get sorted into gametes as complete units, so without crossing over, every gene sitting on a given chromosome would travel together as a fixed package, generation after generation, exactly as it was inherited from one parent. Crossing over breaks up that package. It lets a chromatid end up carrying a mix of maternal and paternal alleles rather than a pure block from just one parent. That mixing is a second, independent source of genetic variation in gametes, on top of whatever variation comes from how whole chromosomes get sorted, and it is the reason siblings can differ from each other even for genes that sit on the very same chromosome.

A simple way to picture this is with two genes sitting near each other on one chromosome, one with alleles A and a, another with alleles B and b. Suppose a person inherited a chromosome carrying A and B together from one parent, and the homologous chromosome carrying a and b together from the other parent. If no crossover occurs between these two loci, the chromatids that go into gametes stay as the original AB and ab combinations, called parental types. But if a crossover happens between the two loci, one of the resulting chromatids can carry A together with b, and its partner can carry a together with B, combinations that did not exist on either original chromosome. These are called recombinant chromatids.

Crossing over happens during prophase I, after synapsis has physically brought the homologous chromosomes close enough together for their DNA to be exchanged. The point on the chromosome where this exchange took place does not disappear once the swap is finished. It leaves behind a visible, physical connection between the two chromatids, which is exactly what a chiasma is, the subject of the next chapter.
